Adoption (Soteriology)
uh-DOP-shun
noun (soteriology)
From Greek huiothesia (placing as a son). The act of God's free grace by which justified believers are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God. Westminster Confession XII; Romans 8:15-17; Galatians 4:4-7; the highest privilege of the gospel.

📖 Biblical Definition

From Greek huiothesia (the placing or setting of one as a son); the act of God's free grace by which justified believers are received into the family of God and granted all the privileges of the sons of God. The Westminster Confession (XII) describes adoption: All those that are justified, God vouchsafeth, in and for his only Son Jesus Christ, to make partakers of the grace of adoption: by which they are taken into the number, and enjoy the liberties and privileges of the children of God; have his name put upon them; receive the Spirit of adoption; have access to the throne of grace with boldness; are enabled to cry, Abba, Father; are pitied, protected, provided for, and chastened by him as by a father; yet never cast off, but sealed to the day of redemption, and inherit the promises, as heirs of everlasting salvation. The biblical foundation: (1) Romans 8:15-17, ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father... and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; (2) Galatians 4:4-7, God sent forth His Son to redeem them under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons... wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ; (3) John 1:12, as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God; (4) 1 John 3:1, Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God. Adoption is distinguished from justification (justification is the forensic declaration of righteous standing; adoption is the gracious reception into the family of God as sons), though the two are inseparable and simultaneous. Adoption is among the highest privileges of the gospel: the believer is not merely acquitted (justification) but received as a beloved son into the family of God, with the Spirit of adoption, access to the Father, the Father's care and discipline, and the inheritance of eternal life. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of adoption: the justified believer is received by God's free grace into the family of God as a son, granted all the privileges of sonship; this is a distinct and glorious benefit of redemption, the believer crying Abba, Father by the Spirit of adoption, and inheriting all things as an heir of God and joint-heir with Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

From Greek huiothesia (placing as a son); God's act of free grace by which justified believers are received into the family of God with all the privileges of sons; Westminster XII; Romans 8:15-17; Galatians 4:4-7; the Spirit of adoption crying Abba, Father; among the highest privileges of the gospel.

ADOPTION (SOTERIOLOGY), n. (Greek huiothesia, placing as a son) The act of God's free grace by which justified believers are received into the family of God with all the privileges of the sons of God. Westminster XII: they are taken into the number of God's children, have His name put upon them, receive the Spirit of adoption, have access to the throne of grace with boldness, cry Abba, Father, are pitied, protected, provided for, and chastened as by a father, never cast off, and inherit the promises. Foundation: Romans 8:15-17 (the Spirit of adoption... heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ); Galatians 4:4-7; John 1:12; 1 John 3:1. Distinguished from justification (forensic standing) yet inseparable; among the highest privileges of the gospel.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 8:15-17 — "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father... And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ."

Galatians 4:4-5 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons."

John 1:12 — "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name."

1 John 3:1 — "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Adoption is the gracious reception of justified believers into the family of God as sons; the principal mishandling is the neglect of adoption as a distinct benefit, collapsing it into justification or treating it as a mere metaphor rather than a real change of status and relationship.

expand to see more

Adoption as a soteriological doctrine does not undergo lexical corruption. The principal mishandling is the neglect of adoption as a distinct and glorious benefit of redemption. Some treatments collapse adoption into justification (treating it as merely an aspect of the forensic declaration) or treat it as a mere metaphor; the Reformed doctrine holds adoption as a distinct benefit, a real change of status and relationship: the justified believer is not merely acquitted (justification, the forensic declaration of righteous standing) but received into the family of God as a beloved son (adoption, the gracious reception into sonship). The two are distinct yet inseparable and simultaneous. The patriarchal-Reformed reader recovers the substantive doctrine of adoption as among the highest privileges of the gospel. The believer who was an alienated enemy, a child of wrath, a slave under the law, is by God's free grace received into the family of God as a beloved son; he has the name of God put upon him; he receives the Spirit of adoption, by whom he cries Abba, Father (Romans 8:15); he has bold access to the throne of grace; he is pitied, protected, provided for, and lovingly disciplined by the Father; he is never cast off but sealed to the day of redemption; and he inherits all things as an heir of God and joint-heir with Christ (Romans 8:17). The wonder of adoption is captured in 1 John 3:1: Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God. The patriarchal-Reformed reader, with his deep emphasis on fatherhood and sonship, finds in the doctrine of adoption the gospel's crowning relational privilege: the believer is a son of the heavenly Father, brought into the family by the grace of the gospel, secure in the Father's love forever.
